In a comprehensive study of growth patterns in the Guri sea catfish (Genidens genidens) from a coastal lagoon system, researchers documented that individuals reached an ultimate total length of 42.2 cm [Li = 42.2 cm], a size that places this species among the larger members of the Ariidae family in South American estuaries. Length-frequency distributions obtained from monthly trawl surveys over a three-year period indicated that asymptotic body size was approached gradually, with the largest specimens captured in the deeper, more saline channels of the lagoon. This ultimate length serves as a key reference point for understanding the species' ecological role as a demersal predator within the benthic community. Males and females did not differ substantially in maximum recorded length, suggesting a monomorphic growth trajectory in this population. The relatively modest maximal dimensions of Genidens genidens, compared to some marine ariids, may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the variable salinity and temperature regimes characteristic of its brackish-water habitat, where food resources can fluctuate seasonally.

Puberty in Genidens genidens occurs at a total length of 11.8 cm [Lp = 11.8 cm], a threshold that corresponds to approximately the end of the first year of life in most individuals examined. Histological analysis of gonad tissue from a size-stratified sample of 240 fish revealed the onset of gametogenesis coincided closely with this length, marking the transition from the juvenile stage to reproductive competence. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty was estimated at 14 grams [Wwp = 14 grams], a relatively low body mass that reflects the species' investment in early maturation. This reproductive strategy, where puberty is reached at less than one-third of the ultimate length, is consistent with an opportunistic life-history pattern observed in other ariid catfishes inhabiting unpredictable estuarine environments. Early maturation allows individuals to contribute to the next generation before facing the elevated mortality risks associated with larger body size in habitats where predation pressure from piscivorous birds and larger fishes is considerable.

The wet weight at birth for Guri sea catfish neonates is 1.15 grams [Wwb = 1.15 grams], a value derived from the substantial yolk reserves contained within eggs measuring approximately 13 mm in diameter. Egg diameter measurements taken from gravid females confirmed that the spherical, demersal eggs are among the largest recorded for ariid catfishes, consistent with the production of well-developed offspring at hatching. This substantial per-offspring investment, corresponding to a neonatal mass of 1.15 grams [Wwb = 1.15 grams], exemplifies the oral-brooding reproductive mode characteristic of the Ariidae, where males incubate the developing embryos in the buccal cavity for several weeks. The large egg size and correspondingly large hatchling mass are thought to enhance early survival by producing larvae that are relatively advanced at first exogenous feeding, reducing the period of vulnerability to planktonic predators. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this heavy investment per offspring is achieved at the cost of reduced fecundity per spawning event.

Adult body mass data collected from the lagoon population demonstrated that the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 707 grams [Wwi = approximately 707 grams], with the heaviest individuals approaching the upper end of this size range. This asymptotic mass, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large dataset of over 800 specimens, confirms that Genidens genidens attains a robust body condition consistent with its benthic feeding habits, which include crustaceans, polychaetes, and small fishes. The length-weight relationship revealed a positive allometric growth pattern, meaning that weight increases at a faster rate relative to length as the fish approach their ultimate size. This asymptotic mass of 707 grams [Wwi = 707 grams] is somewhat lower than a theoretical estimate based on the ultimate length using a general ariid equation, suggesting that local environmental conditions or intraspecific competition may constrain maximum mass in this particular estuary. This value represents an important benchmark for calculating the species' bioenergetic demands and its role in energy flow through the lagoon food web.

Laboratory-based observations of reproductive output and longevity were conducted at a stable thermal regime of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], conditions that closely matched the annual mean water temperature of the species' natural habitat. Under these controlled conditions, the maximum reproduction rate was expressed through a clutch size of 17 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 17 eggs per spawning event], with females capable of producing a single such clutch each year [F_R_i = single such clutch each year]. This reproductive schedule, coupled with the large egg size noted earlier, underscores an energetically conservative approach to offspring production. The same thermal conditions were associated with a maximum recorded lifespan of 36 years [am = 36 years] in captive individuals, an impressive longevity for a fish of this body size that likely contributes to the species' population stability in fluctuating estuarine environments at a temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. The combination of low annual fecundity and extreme longevity positions Genidens genidens at the slow end of the life-history continuum among ariid catfishes.
